20849:
In the early church two centres became associated with different styles. In Alexandria, Origen (c. 185-254) taught that Scripture, like a human being, has a body, a soul and a spirit: a literal sense, a moral sense and a spiritual sense (On First Principles 4.2.4). Where the literal sense seemed unworthy of God or impossible, he looked for a spiritual meaning.

In Antioch, teachers such as Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia and John Chrysostom pressed for close attention to history, grammar and the author's purpose. They accepted typology but spoke of theoria, a spiritual insight that grows out of the historical meaning rather than leaping past it. Theodore was cautious about reading many psalms as directly about Christ.

Many scholars, notably Frances Young, now argue that the contrast is overdrawn: both schools used typology and spiritual reading, and their differences were partly about rhetorical style and theological debates. The two names remain a useful shorthand for two instincts every reader has: 'see Christ everywhere' and 'first hear what the text meant then'.
20851:
In the medieval West, reading settled into four 'senses' of Scripture, sometimes called the quadriga (a four-horse chariot). John Cassian (c. 420) gave the classic example of Jerusalem (Conferences 14.8): literally a city in Judea; allegorically the church; morally (tropologically) the human soul; and anagogically (pointing upward) the heavenly city of God.

A short medieval rhyme, usually credited to Augustine of Dacia (c. 1260), summed it up: the letter teaches what happened, allegory what to believe, the moral sense what to do, and anagogy where we are heading.

Thomas Aquinas insisted that all the spiritual senses are founded on the literal one, and that arguments for doctrine must come from the literal sense alone (Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10). The Catholic Catechism still teaches the four senses with that priority (paragraphs 115-119).

The Reformers pushed hard for the 'literal sense', meaning the sense the author intended, including figures of speech. Yet Luther and Calvin kept a strong typology, especially seeing Christ in the Psalms and the sacrificial system. Eastern Orthodox reading never formalised the four senses but continues the patristic habit of reading the Old Testament in the light of Christ, especially in its hymns.
20852: Guardrails for reading types and symbols
20853:
Most interpreters, across traditions, use some version of these checks.

1. Plain sense first. Ask what the passage meant to its first readers before asking what it foreshadows.

2. New Testament warrant. Is the link made explicitly in the New Testament (Passover, bronze serpent, Jonah, Melchizedek), implied (Joseph rejected by his brothers then exalted), traditional (Isaac carrying the wood), or only someone's idea? The more speculative, the lighter the weight. The Anglican bishop Herbert Marsh (1820s) argued we should only call something a type if the New Testament does; most now think that is too narrow, since the apostles were showing a method, not giving a complete list.

3. Real correspondence. The type and antitype should share a significant pattern, not just a word or a colour.

4. Escalation. The fulfilment is greater than the shadow: 'a greater than Jonas is here', 'a greater than Solomon' (Matt 12:41-42). If the 'antitype' is no greater, it is probably just a parallel.

5. No doctrine from symbols alone. A teaching should rest on clear statements; types illustrate and deepen it.

6. Watch for differences. Every type also differs from Christ, and noticing the differences keeps us honest (Hebrews does this constantly: Heb 7:23-28).
20854: How Christ-centred should Old Testament reading be? Some (redemptive-historical and many patristic readers) see Christ foreshadowed across the whole Old Testament; others warn that this can mute the text's own voice and its meaning for Israel. See /debates/christocentric-hermeneutic.
20856:
The type: in Egypt each Israelite household killed a spotless lamb, put its blood on the doorposts, and the destroyer passed over those houses (Exod 12:1-13). No bone of the lamb was to be broken (Exod 12:46). The meal was repeated every year as a memorial.

The antitype: John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' (John 1:29). John's Gospel places Jesus' death at the time the Passover lambs were sacrificed and notes that none of his bones were broken, citing the Passover rule (John 19:36). Paul says plainly, 'Christ our passover is sacrificed for us' (1 Cor 5:7). Jesus himself reshaped the Passover meal into the Lord's Supper (Luke 22:14-20).

Warrant: explicit. Correspondence: a substitute death, protection by blood, deliverance from slavery, a memorial meal. Escalation: from one night's rescue in Egypt to deliverance from sin and death for the world.

Differences: the Passover lamb was not, in Exodus, mainly a sin offering; it was a sign of protection and belonging. Readers who notice this see that the New Testament gathers several Old Testament sacrifices into one picture of Christ.
20857: Worked example: the bronze serpent, and when a symbol becomes an idol
20858:
The type: in the wilderness, Israel complained, and poisonous snakes bit the people. God told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole; whoever looked at it lived (Num 21:4-9).

The antitype: Jesus tells Nicodemus that as Moses lifted up the serpent, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that whoever believes may have eternal life (John 3:14-15). The correspondence is striking: the cure looks like the curse, it is lifted up, and the response is simply to look in trust. Early Christians such as Justin Martyr developed the link further (Dialogue with Trypho 91, 94).

A warning comes in the Old Testament itself. Centuries later Israel was burning incense to the bronze serpent, which had been named Nehushtan, and King Hezekiah broke it in pieces (2 Kgs 18:4). The object that once pointed to God's mercy had become an object of worship. Types and symbols are signposts; treating the sign as the destination is the danger.
20859: Worked example: the sign of Jonah
20860:
The type: Jonah was swallowed by a great fish and was in its belly three days and three nights before being spat out on dry land (Jonah 1:17, Jonah 2:10). He then preached to Nineveh, which repented (Jonah 3:5).

The antitype: asked for a sign, Jesus says no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was three days and nights in the fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and nights 'in the heart of the earth' (Matt 12:39-40). He adds that Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and 'a greater than Jonas is here' (Matt 12:41). Luke's version focuses on Jonah as a sign to Nineveh through his preaching (Luke 11:29-32).

Escalation is explicit. The 'three days and three nights' phrase raises a question, since Jesus was in the tomb from Friday to Sunday. Many scholars note that Jewish reckoning counted any part of a day as a day, so this is a set phrase rather than 72 hours; a minority argue for a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion.

Whether Jonah's story is literal history or a God-inspired parable is debated among Christians; Jesus' use of it as a type works either way for some readers, while others argue that his comparison with the real men of Nineveh implies history.
20861: Three days and three nights: most interpreters read it as an idiom for parts of three days (compare Esth 4:16 with Esth 5:1). A minority propose a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion to fit 72 hours.
20863:
Revelation is full of numbers, and nearly all interpreters agree that at least some are symbolic. Revelation itself explains symbols at times: the seven stars are the angels of seven churches and the lampstands are the churches (Rev 1:20).

Seven suggests completeness (seven churches, seals, trumpets, bowls), echoing the seven days of creation. Twelve recalls the tribes and the apostles; the New Jerusalem has twelve gates and twelve foundations (Rev 21:12-14) and measures 12,000 stadia (Rev 21:16). The 144,000 (Rev 7:4, Rev 14:1) is 12 x 12 x 1,000; many read it as the whole people of God, others as a literal number of Jewish believers or a special group. Right after hearing the number, John sees 'a great multitude, which no man could number' (Rev 7:9), which many take as the same group seen differently.

666 is called 'the number of a man' (Rev 13:18). In ancient practice letters had number values (gematria). Many scholars note that 'Nero Caesar' written in Hebrew letters adds up to 666, and a variant reading 616, known to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.1) and found in an early papyrus, matches the Latin spelling. Others read 666 as falling short of seven again and again. The 1,000 years (Rev 20:2-7) is read literally by premillennialists and symbolically by amillennialists and many postmillennialists.

The caution: Revelation's numbers invite us to see patterns of completeness, God's people and evil's imitation, not to calculate dates or decode news headlines.
20864: Myth: 'Hidden number codes in the Bible predict modern events.' Fact: 'Bible code' claims (equidistant letter sequences) have been shown by statisticians to produce similar 'predictions' from any long text. Revelation's numbers are open symbols in the text, explained by Old Testament background, not secret codes.
20865: Some well-known types and how strong the link is
20874: Death through one, life through the other
20882: Those who ate died; this bread gives eternal life
20887: Death and resurrection; preaching to Gentiles
20898: Saving eight to saving all who believe
20901: Saving Egypt to saving the world
20905: Ram substituted; the Son not spared
20909: Speculative; best treated as an illustration
20911: The whole Old Testament is read in the light of Christ; typology is woven through liturgy and hymns, and spiritual readings are welcomed within the rule of faith.
20912: The four senses of Scripture remain valid, all grounded in the literal sense, with the church's tradition guiding spiritual interpretation (Catechism 115-119).
20914: Typology is a key thread of the Bible's single story of redemption; the literal-historical sense controls, and types are recognised by New Testament patterns, with debate over how far beyond explicit warrant to go.
20916: Typology is a way early Jewish and Christian communities reread their scriptures; it tells us about the New Testament writers' convictions rather than about the original meaning of Old Testament texts.
20919: Is Paul's reading of Sarah and Hagar in Galatians 4 typology or allegory, and does it matter?
20920: Can we find types the New Testament does not mention, or should we stop where it stops?
20921: Did Old Testament authors know their stories foreshadowed something greater?
20922: How should the numbers in Revelation shape the way we read its timeline?
20923: Where is the line between a helpful illustration and an over-reading?
20925: The Bible says God is sovereign and that we are responsible, that we are saved by faith and that faith without works is dead, that Jesus is equal with the Father and that the Father is greater. Are these contradictions, and how should we live with them?
20926: The Bible often puts two truths side by side that seem to pull against each other. A paradox is an apparent clash between two statements that are both true in their proper sense; a contradiction is when two statements cannot both be true in the same sense at the same time. Christians have handled these tensions in several ways: by careful distinctions that show the clash is only apparent (harmonisation), by accepting both truths without fully reconciling them (what J. I. Packer called an antinomy), by confessing that God is beyond our concepts (Eastern 'apophatic' theology), or by reading the different voices as a deliberate conversation within Scripture. Sceptics argue that some tensions are real contradictions between different human authors. Living well with paradox usually means holding both truths in practice, rather than letting one quietly cancel the other.
20927: A paradox is an apparent contradiction; a real contradiction affirms and denies the same thing in the same sense at the same time.
20928: Many biblical tensions (sovereignty and responsibility, faith and works, divine and human in Christ) are central to Christian faith, not marginal puzzles.
20929: J. I. Packer's 'antinomy' means two well-attested truths we cannot yet reconcile but must both believe and act on.
20930: G. K. Chesterton argued that Christianity's health lies in keeping opposite truths both at full strength rather than blending them into a weak compromise.
20931: Eastern Orthodox apophatic theology says God exceeds our concepts, so some tensions are signs of mystery, not error.
20932: Harmonisation and literary readings help, but each has a risk: forced explanations on one side, or giving up the unity of Scripture on the other.
20933: In practice, most paradoxes are 'lived' by praying as if all depends on God and acting as if all depends on us, or similar double commitments.
20934: Why the Bible holds truths in tension
20935:
Scripture often says two things that seem hard to fit together. Joseph's brothers meant evil, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). Jesus was handed over by God's set purpose, yet the people who crucified him were guilty (Acts 2:23). Paul tells believers to work out their salvation because God works in them (Phil 2:12-13). Jesus says whoever wants to save his life will lose it (Matt 16:25), and Paul says, 'when I am weak, then am I strong' (2 Cor 12:10).

Some tensions sit next to each other on purpose. Proverbs says 'Answer not a fool according to his folly' and in the next verse 'Answer a fool according to his folly' (Prov 26:4-5). The editors plainly saw the clash; the point is that wisdom means knowing which applies when.

There are several reasons for this. God is greater than human understanding (Isa 55:8-9). Reality itself is complex, and truths about persons, love and freedom rarely fit into one formula. And Scripture was written over many centuries in many genres, so it speaks from more than one angle.
20937:
In logic, a contradiction affirms and denies the same thing in the same sense at the same time: 'this door is open' and 'this door is not open'. Both cannot be true. A paradox is a statement or pair of statements that seem contradictory but, on reflection, may both be true because they speak in different senses or about different aspects.

'I am the vine' and 'I am the door' do not contradict, because they are images. 'My Father is greater than I' (John 14:28) and 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30) were explained by the early church as speaking of Christ's human nature or his role as Son on the one hand, and his divine nature or shared being on the other.

The key questions are: are the two statements using words in the same sense? Are they about the same subject in the same respect? Are they answering the same question? Many apparent contradictions dissolve under these questions; some remain mysterious; and critics argue that some are real.
20938: Two opposite myths. 'Paradox is just a polite word for contradiction' ignores that many paradoxes rest on real distinctions. 'Calling it a mystery ends the discussion' ignores that Christian thinkers have always worked hard to understand mysteries as far as they can.
20939: Antinomy: J. I. Packer on sovereignty and evangelism
20940:
In *Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God* (1961), the Anglican theologian J. I. Packer asked how a Calvinist, who believes God chooses who will be saved, can evangelise urgently. His answer, in chapter 2, used the word 'antinomy'. He defined it (in paraphrase) as an apparent incompatibility between two truths that are each clearly taught and well grounded, which we cannot reconcile with our present understanding but must both accept.

Packer compared it to light behaving both as waves and as particles: physicists accept both because the evidence requires it. In the same way, Scripture teaches both divine sovereignty (Rom 9:15-16, Eph 1:11) and human responsibility to repent and believe (Acts 17:30, Rom 10:13-14). He urged Christians to pray as those who depend entirely on God and to preach as those who must persuade people.

Critics come from two directions. Some Reformed thinkers (for example Gordon Clark) objected that 'antinomy' sounds like an admission of irrationality and preferred to say the tension is resolved in God's mind and partly in ours. Arminian and Wesleyan theologians argue that the tension is largely of Calvinism's own making and is better resolved by understanding election through foreknowledge and grace that enables free response. Many compatibilists, such as D. A. Carson, defend the coherence of the two truths more fully than Packer did.
20941: Whether sovereignty and responsibility are an antinomy, a coherent compatibilism, or a false tension created by a particular view of election is one of the oldest debates in theology. See /debates/soteriology.
20942: Chesterton: keeping both truths at full strength
20943:
In *Orthodoxy* (1908), G. K. Chesterton described his discovery that Christianity was attacked from opposite sides: too gloomy and too optimistic, too meek and too warlike. In chapter 6, 'The Paradoxes of Christianity', he concluded that the faith did not settle for a bland middle point between such opposites. Instead it held both extremes at full strength side by side: intense humility about ourselves and intense dignity as God's image-bearers; fierce hatred of sin and great love for the sinner.

For Chesterton, the doctrine of Christ is the model: not half God and half man, but fully both (John 1:14, Col 2:9). Heresy, in his picture, usually takes one true idea and lets it run without its balancing partner.

Chesterton was writing as a literary apologist, not a technical theologian, and some readers think he made paradox sound easier and more romantic than it is. But his idea that health lies in balance, not dilution, has shaped much popular Christian thinking.
20944: The Eastern way: apophatic theology and mystery
20945:
Eastern Orthodox theology has long stressed 'apophatic' or negative theology: saying what God is not, because God is beyond every human concept. God 'dwells in the light which no man can approach unto' (1 Tim 6:16). Moses drew near 'unto the thick darkness where God was' (Exod 20:21).

Gregory of Nyssa, in his *Life of Moses* (around 390), read Moses' climb into the dark cloud as the soul's growth into God, where knowing God means realising he surpasses knowledge. The writer known as Pseudo-Dionysius (around 500) in *The Mystical Theology* taught that we rise to God by stripping away even our best words. In the 20th century Vladimir Lossky, in *The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church*, argued that the doctrines of the Trinity and of Christ are 'antinomies' that guard mystery rather than explain it away.

On this view, tensions such as one God in three persons are not puzzles waiting for a clever solution but boundaries that keep us from shrinking God. Western theology has its own apophatic tradition (Augustine, Aquinas, the medieval mystics), but it has usually been more willing to press for rational explanation. Critics warn that apophatic language can become an excuse for vagueness; its defenders reply that it always goes together with positive (cataphatic) confession of what God has revealed.
20947:
Harmonisation means showing that two statements fit together once we read them carefully. Augustine wrote *The Harmony of the Gospels* (around 400) to show that differences between the four Gospels were not contradictions.

A classic case is faith and works. Paul says a person is justified by faith 'without the deeds of the law' (Rom 3:28), using Abraham as his example (Rom 4:2-3). James says 'by works a man is justified, and not by faith only' (Jas 2:24), also citing Abraham (Jas 2:21). Most interpreters, Catholic and Protestant, argue that the two use 'works' and 'justify' differently: Paul rejects works of the law as a way to earn standing with God, while James rejects a 'faith' that is only words and shows that real faith proves itself in action. Paul himself says believers are created 'unto good works' (Eph 2:8-10). Catholic and Protestant theologians still differ over how works relate to final justification.

Harmonisation is a natural reading strategy; we do it with any trusted witness. Its risk is forcing. A famous example: the Reformation-era scholar Andreas Osiander is reported to have proposed that Peter denied Jesus six times to fit every Gospel detail. Most harmonisers today prefer to admit where we do not know, rather than invent solutions the texts do not suggest.
20948: Myth: 'Paul and James flatly contradict each other, and Luther threw James out.' Fact: most interpreters across traditions see the two addressing different errors with different senses of the words. Luther did call James 'an epistle of straw' compared with Paul's letters in his 1522 preface and doubted its authority, but he kept it in his Bible.
20949: Literary and critical readings: a conversation in the canon
20950:
Many scholars read some tensions as deliberate dialogue. Proverbs teaches that wise living generally brings blessing; Job and Ecclesiastes push back that life does not always work that way (Job 21:7, Eccl 9:11). Brevard Childs's 'canonical' approach reads such books as placed together on purpose, so that each corrects and completes the others. Walter Brueggemann describes Israel's 'core testimony' about God's faithfulness alongside a 'countertestimony' of lament and protest, both kept in Scripture.

Historical-critical scholars also explain some tensions by different sources or later rethinking. 2 Samuel says the Lord moved David to number Israel (2 Sam 24:1); the later Chronicles says Satan provoked him (1 Chr 21:1). Many scholars see a development in how Israel spoke about evil and God's role. Traditional readers often see layered causation: God permitted, Satan incited, David chose, as in Job 1-2.

Sceptics such as Bart Ehrman (*Jesus, Interrupted*, 2009) argue that some differences are genuine contradictions between human authors and should be accepted as such. Many believing scholars accept the presence of diverse voices but argue that diversity is not the same as contradiction, and that the canon holds them together intentionally.
